{"id": "11:112/q13", "question": "What conduct does do not transgress forbid?", "turns_on": "Whether ṭughyān is read as the inclusive crossing of all limits or a specified kind of excess.", "positions": [{"id": "11:112/q13/p1", "position": "Every departure from God's limits, including excess and neglect, disobedience, oppression, and distortion of commands.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī and Ibn Zayd identify disobedience; al-Wāḥidī, Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ṭabrisī, Qurṭubī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, and Ālūsī state the general limit. {"id": "11:112/q17", "question": "What does God being baṣīr of deeds convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:112/q17/p1", "position": "He sees and knows every deed, including hidden obedience and disobedience, and recompenses them.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī says nothing escapes God; Ibn ʿAbbās in al-Wāḥidī adds that He knew acts before they occurred. {"id": "11:112/q18", "question": "Why close with God's sight of deeds?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:112/q18/p1", "position": "It warns against concealed disobedience and gives God's knowledge vivid force.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says seeing conveys clear, powerful knowledge even of transgression people hide; Bayḍāwī and Ālūsī connect it causally with the command, prohibition, and recompense."}]}
{"id": "11:112/q19", "question": "What legal method does the command to stand firm support?", "turns_on": "Whether text-grounded analogy can count as obedience to the command and whether conjunction imposes legal sequence.", "positions": [{"id": "11:112/q19/p1", "position": "Follow the explicit order of divine texts, without specifying general wording by analogy or juristic preference.", "reasons": "Rāzī uses commanded steadfastness to require the stated sequence in ablution and like livestock for zakāt; he objects to qualifying a general text by analogy. Bayḍāwī likewise bars alteration by analogy or juristic preference. Ālūsī reports the inference but distinguishes analogy based on textual causes as authorized ijtihād; he rejects the ablution-order proof because it would impose order on every pair joined by wa, such as prayer and alms, and unfairly condemn Ḥanafīs who do not require that order."}, {"id": "11:112/q19/p2", "position": "Fidelity to texts also permits analogy grounded in textual causes.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports this qualification as authorized ijtihād and objects to Rāzī's blanket rejection of specifying general texts by analogy, particularly its ablution-order and Ḥanafī implications."}]}

{"id": "11:112/q22", "question": "What is reported about the Prophet's burden on receiving this command?", "turns_on": "The reports describe different effects of the verse, with varying sura names in the graying account.", "positions": [{"id": "11:112/q22/p1", "position": "Ibn ʿAbbās called it the hardest verse for the Prophet, connecting it to his graying.", "reasons": "Jishumī, Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, Rāzī, Qurṭubī, Biqāʿī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, and Ṭabāṭabāʾ transmit this. {"id": "11:112/q23", "question": "Which suras did the Prophet say made him gray?", "turns_on": "The transmitted wording names Hūd alone, Hūd with sister suras, Hūd with al-Wāqiʿa, or those suras together with earlier nations' fates.", "positions": [{"id": "11:112/q23/p1", "position": "Hūd and its sister suras.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Rāzī, Qurṭubī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, al-Ālūsī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, Ṭabāṭabāʾ, and Kuryolu report this wording or describe it as familiar. Qurṭubī says companions noticed his rapid graying; al-Ālūsī notes other wordings are compatible."}, {"id": "11:112/q23/p2", "position": "Hūd alone.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī and Nasafī cite the shortened saying; al-Ālūsī says this wording need not conflict with fuller reports, while al-Kashf questions singling Hūd out when sister suras lack an explicit uprightness command."}, {"id": "11:112/q23/p3", "position": "Hūd and al-Wāqiʿa.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī and Ṭabāṭabāʾ transmit this wording with Ibn ʿAbbās; Ṭabāṭabāʾ says al-Wāqiʿa lacks a parallel command and may share the theme of Resurrection instead."}, {"id": "11:112/q23/p4", "position": "Hūd, its sister suras, and the fate of earlier nations.", "reasons": "Ālūsī cites an Ibn ʿAsākir transmission through Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad from his father and explains that fuller and shorter versions can coexist."}]}
{"id": "11:112/q24", "question": "What part of Hūd was said to have made him gray, and why?", "turns_on": "Whether the report points to the command's difficulty, previous nations' fates, the community's risk, or shared eschatological material.", "positions": [{"id": "11:112/q24/p1", "position": "The command to stand firm as ordered, because fulfilling it is especially demanding.", "reasons": "A dream in Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Rāzī, Qurṭubī, and Qāshānī has the Prophet identify this verse rather than the destroyed peoples' stories; Qāshānī says an ʿārif saw the dream, while Qurṭubī names Abū ʿAlī al-Sarrī in al-Sulamī's account. Ibn ʿĀshūr and Kuryolu likewise cite the identification; Bayḍāwī links Hūd's effect to the difficulty of uprightness. Al-Shihāb says the verse summarizes Hūd's guidance and raises fear of falling short of its demands without impugning infallibility."}, {"id": "11:112/q24/p2", "position": "Fear that earlier peoples' punishment might overtake his community.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this the well-known explanation; al-Ālūsī's expanded report includes what befell earlier nations, while Ṭabāṭabāʾ says the grave address after their destruction heightens the warning."}, {"id": "11:112/q24/p3", "position": "Concern for his community because their steadfastness is vulnerable.", "reasons": "Elmalılı connects the singular positive command and plural prohibitions to risk among the community and says this rhetorical feature aged the Prophet."}, {"id": "11:112/q24/p4", "position": "The Resurrection scenes common to the named suras may explain the effect.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾ proposes this because al-Wāqiʿa has no equivalent command to stand firm; al-Kashf as reported by Ālūsī likewise questions singling out uprightness when the sister suras do not mention it."}]}
{"id": "11:112/q25", "question": "What other reports illustrate steadfastness and moderation?", "turns_on": "The reports illustrate distinct settings and outcomes rather than competing accounts of one event.", "positions": [{"id": "11:112/q25/p1", "position": "A report from ʿUmar says extreme prayer and fasting do not attain steadfastness if people prefer two over one.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī reports it under the Prophet's authority through ʿUmar; the note does not explain the final phrase further."}, {"id": "11:112/q25/p2", "position": "The Prophet taught that religion is easy and urged moderate practice without overburdening oneself.", "reasons": "Abū Hurayra's report in Baghawī adds rejoicing and seeking help at times of day and night."}, {"id": "11:112/q25/p3", "position": "Earlier believers held firm under torture, and the Prophet promised Islam's eventual completion.", "reasons": "Khabbāb's report in Biqāʿī describes saws and iron combs, safety on the road from Ṣanʿāʾ to Ḥaḍramawt, and the Prophet's rebuke of impatience."}]}
{"id": "11:112/q26", "question": "What readings and analyses of lammā in the neighboring verse are reported?", "turns_on": "The vocalization of in and kull, the doubled mīm, whether lammā is a noun, particle, contraction, or ellipsis, and the limits of Arabic usage.", "positions": [{"id": "11:112/q26/p1", "position": "The transmitted tanwīn reading can treat lammā as a verbal noun or adjective describing comprehensive fulfillment.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī compares aklan lammā; al-Ṭabrisī says an adjectival analysis needs kull annexed to an indefinite noun and has no governing element for a circumstantial reading. Ibn Jinnī likens emphatic fulfillment to qiyāman; a proposal derives it from gathering on the pattern faʿlā, like tatrā, with al-Zuhrī's tanwīn supporting it."}, {"id": "11:112/q26/p2", "position": "Lammā may contract li-man mā, dropping one of three mīms.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ cites a poem for this."}, {"id": "11:112/q26/p3", "position": "Lammā may mean illā, an exception particle.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj proposes it; al-Farrāʾ and Abū ʿAlī object that this use belongs to oaths. Al-Ṭabrisī reports a related reading wa-in kulla illā la-yuwaffiyannahum, allowing illā as extra with lightened in, and explains a poem's extra illā as saying time confuses its people and frustrates petitioners."}, {"id": "11:112/q26/p4", "position": "Its doubled form may be an emphatically doubled light form.", "reasons": "Al-Māzinī proposes this; al-Zajjāj objects that Arabic only weakens a doubled form under poetic necessity, rather than doubling a light form. Al-Kisāʾī says he cannot explain the doubling, and Abū ʿAlī accepts the difficulty."}, {"id": "11:112/q26/p5", "position": "An omitted phrase may explain it: each will be repaid for what they did.", "reasons": "ʿAlī ibn Abī al-Ṭayyib supplies wa-in kullan lammā ʿamilū la-yuwaffiyannahum rabbuka aʿmālahum and cites poetry illustrating ellipsis."}, {"id": "11:112/q26/p6", "position": "With light in and nominative kull, it can be an adjective of indefinite kull or amount to each certainly being repaid.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī says this would ease the analysis, parallel to 43:35; al-Ṭabrisī says a definite annexation blocks it. Al-Ṭabrisī rejects proposals using inserted wa-in hum illā or explanatory kullan, and says a doubled mīm with either form of in yields none of the known senses of lam, ḥīn, or illā."}]}
{"id": "11:112/q27", "question": "What other neighboring word forms and meanings are noted?", "turns_on": "The notes concern separate neighboring words and give no dispute beyond dialect variation.", "positions": [{"id": "11:112/q27/p1", "position": "The readings of zulan are dialect variants, and the word is accusative as a time adverb.", "reasons": "Jishumī says the common zulafan has ḍamma on zāy and fatḥa on lām, while Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn Muḥayṣin, and Mujāhid vocalize it differently; he also gives its adverbial case."}, {"id": "11:112/q27/p2", "position": "Mirya is doubt despite clear evidence; a share is an allotted portion; disagreement can be contradictory or validly varied.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī illustrates valid difference by judgments about facing the qibla and includes istiqāma as staying straight and transgression as excess in corruption."}, {"id": "11:112/q27/p3", "position": "Readers vary the kāf vowel in tarkunū, with rounded kāf a dialect form for settling or being content.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports this alongside the final verb's readings."}]}

{"id": "11:112/q29", "question": "How are quiescent hamzas like the one in fastāqim eased?", "turns_on": "Whether connected quiescent word-initial hamza is treated like other medial hamzas and what the transmission records.", "positions": [{"id": "11:112/q29/p1", "position": "They are replaced by the homorganic long vowel and count as medial when joined to the preceding word.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī gives wāw after ḍamma, yāʾ after kasra, and alif after fatḥa; Abū ʿAmr, Abū Jaʿfar, and Warsh are reported to ease these cases without disagreement. {"id": "11:112/q30", "question": "What happens to the hāʾ after easing hamza in cited forms?", "turns_on": "Whether the incidental yāʾ after hamza easing affects the preceding hāʾ.", "positions": [{"id": "11:112/q30/p1", "position": "Some give the hāʾ a kasra by analogy with forms followed by yāʾ.", "reasons": "Abū Bakr ibn Mujāhid, Abū al-Ṭayyib ibn Ghalbūn, and his son apply this to anbihim and nabbiʾhum, comparing fīhim and yuʾtīhim."}, {"id": "11:112/q30/p2", "position": "Most retain its ḍamma because the resulting yāʾ is incidental.", "reasons": "Ibn Mihrān, Makkī, al-Mahdawī, Ibn Sufyān, and most readers take this line; Ibn Ghalbūn accepts either pronunciation."}]}

{"id": "12:26/q01", "question": "What does Joseph say she did?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:26/q01/p1", "position": "She sought to seduce Joseph, while he refused and fled.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj states the reversal; al-Baghawi and Study Quran specify illicit sex and refusal; Ibn Kathir and al-Suddi describe her pursuit and pulling his shirt."}]}
{"id": "12:26/q02", "question": "Why did Joseph disclose her pursuit?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:26/q02/p1", "position": "He answered her false accusation to clear himself; without it he would have kept silent.", "reasons": "Mawardi, Kashshaf, Tabarsi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Biqai, Tabatabai and others stress restraint until she accused him. {"id": "12:26/q03", "question": "Why does Joseph say 'she' rather than address her directly?", "turns_on": "Whether a present or mentally present person licenses a third-person pronoun without a previously stated antecedent.", "positions": [{"id": "12:26/q03/p1", "position": "The third person shows modesty, courtesy, and a wish to avoid direct reproach.", "reasons": "Samin calls it good etiquette instead of hādhihi or tilka; Biqai, Abu Hayyan, and Alusi connect it to restraint or turning away."}, {"id": "12:26/q03/p2", "position": "The third-person pronoun can refer to a person physically or mentally present without a prior verbal antecedent.", "reasons": "Ibn Malik states the rule; Siraj al-Bulqini adds sensory or mental presence. Alusi prefers it, citing a litigant's statement, Moses before he is named in 28:26, and the legal force of hiyya taliq."}, {"id": "12:26/q03/p3", "position": "The pronoun has an available contextual antecedent rather than being licensed by presence alone.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan takes hiyya back to the woman's euphemistic ahlik and the pronoun in istajirhu back to Moses; Burhan says the antecedent is clear from the story."}]}
{"id": "12:26/q04", "question": "What does the order of 'she pursued me' convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:26/q04/p1", "position": "Fronting 'she' assigns the pursuit to her and reverses her accusation.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur identifies subject-before-verb restriction in the separated dialogue; Tabatabai calls the answer a reversal contrast."}, {"id": "12:26/q04/p2", "position": "Joseph's plain, unemphatic reply shows calm assurance.", "reasons": "Tabatabai notes the absence of oath or emphatic language: he neither panicked nor flattered her."}]}
{"id": "12:26/q05", "question": "Who or what was the witness from her family?", "turns_on": "Identity depends on whether 'from her family' names a human relative or can describe a sign or creature, and whether the infant-speaker reports outweigh the shirt-based inference.", "positions": [{"id": "12:26/q05/p1", "position": "A wise adult man of her family, with no closer identity established.", "reasons": "Qatada, Ikrima, Hasan, Mujahid and others describe judgment, wisdom, beard, or maturity. Nahhas prefers a royal counselor and argues infant speech would itself settle the case; Jubba'i and Razi similarly argue a miracle would make the shirt test redundant, and that witness ordinarily implies prior knowledge. Nahhas reads 'young' in the infant report broadly; Ibn Abbas is also reported to deny he was a child."}, {"id": "12:26/q05/p2", "position": "Her adult cousin, often described as wise and present with her husband at the door.", "reasons": "Muqatil names Yamlakha ibn her uncle; Tha'labi names Rachel and Qutayfir; Baghawi says Ra'il's paternal cousin. Suddi, Zayd ibn Aslam and others locate him at the door or describe his shirt test. Ibn Ashur adds that he likely initially believed her; Maududi suggests the cousin may have been a judge, though Kuranyolu finds this uncertain."}, {"id": "12:26/q05/p3", "position": "An infant enabled by God to speak.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurayra, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Dahhak, Hilal and other reports place the child in the cradle or house. Tabari and Ibn Jarir prefer this because of a Prophetic infant-speakers report. Ibn Atiyya questions it against the Sahihayn's three and because an infant's speech would alone prove the case; Qurtubi likewise says it is miraculous proof. Tabatabai sees spontaneous 'testimony' as support, while Ahl al-Bayt and Sunni routes transmit the report. Biqai compares a newborn of Yamama who testified to the Prophet."}, {"id": "12:26/q05/p4", "position": "An infant specifically related to her through her mother.", "reasons": "Tha'labi and Baghawi say maternal cousin; Qushayri says maternal uncle's son; Tabrisi specifies her sister's three-month-old boy; Alusi reports 'maternal uncle' itself. The variants differ in exact kinship."}, {"id": "12:26/q05/p5", "position": "An adult associate or adviser of the king.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas says one of the king's intimates; Ibn Ishaq describes an adviser from Itfir's family. Ibn Kathir adds Ibn Ishaq's account that Zulaykha was King Rayyan ibn al-Walid's niece."}, {"id": "12:26/q05/p6", "position": "A judge or appointed arbiter from her family.", "reasons": "Mujahid's reports call him a judge; Mawardi and Qurtubi infer an arbiter was needed for conflicting claims; Wahidi-Wajiz identifies him as her cousin. Kuranyolu reports Maududi's suggestion but doubts certainty."}, {"id": "12:26/q05/p7", "position": "A relative who had seen or heard something of the encounter.", "reasons": "Kashshaf and Alusi report an unseen family observer; Ibn al-Anbari suggests a witness may have heard the woman behind the door or Joseph's words. Jubba'i argues ordinary 'witness' implies prior knowledge."}, {"id": "12:26/q05/p8", "position": "The woman's servant.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan is reported by Tha'labi to identify him as her servant."}, {"id": "12:26/q05/p9", "position": "The shirt and its tear were themselves the witness.", "reasons": "Mujahid and Qatada call the shirt or its condition testimony; Qurtubi notes Arabic attributes speech to objects. Tabari, Abu Bakr, Ibn Atiyya and Alusi object that a shirt cannot be 'from her family'."}, {"id": "12:26/q05/p10", "position": "A created being who was neither human nor jinn.", "reasons": "Mujahid transmits this; Qurtubi and Tabatabai reject it because the verse calls the witness 'from her family'. Ibn Abi Hatim describes another creature created by God."}]}

{"id": "12:26/q07", "question": "What does it mean that the witness 'testified'?", "turns_on": "Whether the word describes formal prior knowledge, inferential judgment, evidentiary function, or a miraculous spontaneous declaration.", "positions": [{"id": "12:26/q07/p1", "position": "He clarified or judged by an inference, with the shirt as actual evidence.", "reasons": "Wahidi-Basit calls witnessing figurative, citing God's testimony to oneness in 3:18 and the public display of disbelief; Mujahid calls it judgment. Ibn Atiyya and Tabatabai distinguish an inferred indication from ordinary perception-based testimony; Asad says he merely proposed the test. The conditional explains the testimony according to Ibn Ashur."}, {"id": "12:26/q07/p2", "position": "His conditional words count as testimony because they confirm Joseph and disprove her.", "reasons": "Kashshaf and Nasafi stress its evidentiary function; Alusi reports the same; Ibn Ashur extends this to the shirt itself; Tabatabai says testimony is a statement and allows the quotation."}, {"id": "12:26/q07/p3", "position": "He may have heard speech or observed the scene and so had prior knowledge.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Anbari proposes words heard behind the door or from Joseph; Jubba'i argues the normal sense of witness requires such prior knowledge, favoring an adult."}, {"id": "12:26/q07/p4", "position": "It may point to a spontaneous utterance by a speaking infant.", "reasons": "Tabatabai suggests that calling the declaration testimony can signal an unconsidered utterance, supporting the cradle report; he compares scripture's witnessing by hearing, sight, skin, and believers in 41:20 and 63:1."}]}
{"id": "12:26/q08", "question": "How is the conditional sentence attached to 'testified'?", "turns_on": "Whether shahida introduces quoted speech or itself denotes the clarifying judgment.", "positions": [{"id": "12:26/q08/p1", "position": "The conditional is direct speech, with an implied 'he said' or an omitted introductory anna.", "reasons": "Farra permits anna before in kāna and compares 4:11 and poetry; Kashshaf takes it as quoted or implied speech; Tabarsi compares the inheritance address; Samin gives Basran implied fa-qāla versus Kufan shahida meaning 'said'; Tabatabai says testimony itself functions as a statement."}, {"id": "12:26/q08/p2", "position": "The conditional is the inferential content of the witness's clarification.", "reasons": "Wahidi-Basit prefers this established commentators' view; Ibn Ashur says the shirt test explains what he testified."}]}
{"id": "12:26/q09", "question": "How does 'a witness from her family' work grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:26/q09/p1", "position": "'From her family' modifies 'witness' and makes the same-root subject informative.", "reasons": "Samin says shahida shāhid without the modifier would be tautological; Farra construes it as 'a speaker from her family'."}]}
{"id": "12:26/q10", "question": "What does the conditional 'if his shirt was torn' mean in time?", "turns_on": "Whether in shifts past-form kāna into a future condition, whether an omitted expression supplies that force, or whether the condition can concern an already past state.", "positions": [{"id": "12:26/q10/p1", "position": "The past form expresses a future condition or future discovery of an already existing tear.", "reasons": "Nahhas says the conditional is jussive despite past form; Abu Ishaq glosses 'if it is known', citing Zuhayr; Kashshaf and Alusi make the discovery future. {"id": "12:26/q11", "question": "How are 'front' and 'back' read and analyzed?", "turns_on": "The vowel and tanwīn on directional nouns, and whether they are indefinite nouns, terminal adverbs with omitted possessors, or fixed names.", "positions": [{"id": "12:26/q11/p1", "position": "The common reading gives front and back ḍamma with tanwīn.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya reports the majority form; he also records other shortened genitive or unmarked endings."}, {"id": "12:26/q11/p2", "position": "Some read min qablu and min duburu with ḍamma and no tanwīn, as terminal adverbs.", "reasons": "Nahhas attributes three ḍammas to Yahya ibn Ya'mar and Ibn Abi Ishaq; Tabrisi adds Nuh al-Qari and Ibn Jinni's suppressed possessor, comparing 30:4; Qurtubi similarly mentions omitted possessors and alternate endings.
